noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: be able to apply the electron-pair repulsion theory to predict the shapes of, and bond angles in, molecules and ions analogous to those in 3.18

primer.text: Ten molecules carry the shape catalogue: BeCl2 linear at 180, BCl3 trigonal planar at 120, methane's perfect tetrahedron at 109.5, ammonia squeezed to 107 by its lone pair, ammonium restored to 109.5, PCl5's bipyramid mixing 120 with 90, and ethene's carbons flat at 120. This note audits each one's electron count and reads off the geometry.

lessons.title: Two deficient classics: BeCl2 and BCl3
lessons.opening: Beryllium chloride and boron trichloride are the textbook cases of incomplete octets wearing elegant geometry. Beryllium brings two valence electrons and spends both on bonds, boron brings three and does the same - no lone pairs either way - so their electron domains spread to the cleanest minimum-repulsion layouts: a straight line at 180 degrees and a flat triangle at 120.
keyPoints: Beryllium has 2 valence electrons, both used for bonds to chlorine, leaving no lone pairs and an electron-deficient centre.
BeCl2 is linear with a bond angle of 180 degrees.
Boron has 3 valence electrons, all used for bonds to chlorine, also electron deficient.
BCl3 is trigonal planar with bond angles of 120 degrees.
Accommodating fewer than 8 outer electrons is exactly what 'electron deficient' means.

low.restatement: Count the bonds, not the octet: two bonds spread straight (180), three spread flat (120) - deficiency does not disturb the geometry.
low.analogy: A two-arm and a three-arm coat rack: arms spread straight or evenly triangular regardless of how empty the rack is.
low.examPointer: Name the deficiency explicitly when drawing BeCl2 or BCl3 - examiners reward the labelled exception.

medium.restatement: With zero lone pairs, the domain geometry is pure: two bonding domains oppose at 180, three repel evenly at 120; the octet shortfall changes the electron count but not the repulsion arithmetic.
medium.analogy: An under-booked hotel still assigns rooms by the same floor plan: fewer guests, same geometry.
medium.examPointer: Quote both angle and shape in one breath: 'linear, 180' and 'trigonal planar, 120'.

check.stem: Why is BeCl2 linear?

options.text: Two bonding domains and no lone pairs spread to opposite sides at 180 degrees
options.explanation: Minimum repulsion for two domains is a straight line.

options.text: Chlorine atoms repel beryllium's full octet
options.explanation: Be has no full octet - it is deficient.

options.text: A lone pair forces the bonds apart
options.explanation: BeCl2 has no lone pairs.

options.text: The chlorines attract each other sideways
options.explanation: Geometry follows domains around the central atom.

check.stem: What shape and angle does BCl3 adopt?

options.explanation: Three even domains spread in a plane.
That is BeCl2's layout.
That needs four domains.
That needs a lone pair.

check.stem: What does 'electron deficient' mean for these central atoms?

options.text: They accommodate fewer than 8 electrons in their outer shell
options.explanation: Be holds 4 bonding electrons, B holds 6.

options.text: They hold more than 8 outer electrons
options.explanation: That is expansion, not deficiency.

options.text: They carry a full negative charge
options.explanation: Neither molecule is charged.

options.text: They have no electrons at all
options.explanation: Both hold several bonding electrons.

check.stem: How many valence electrons does boron bring to BCl3, and where do they go?

options.text: Three - all three form bonds to chlorine, none left as a lone pair
options.explanation: Group 13 supplies three bonding electrons.

options.text: Five - three bond, two stay lone
options.explanation: Boron has no lone pair in BCl3.
Seven belongs to each chlorine atom.
Beryllium is the other central atom.

check.stem: Which statement about the lone pairs in BeCl2 and BCl3 is correct?

options.text: Both molecules have no lone pairs on the central atom
options.explanation: Every valence electron is spent on bonding.
Beryllium's both electrons bond.
Boron's three electrons all bond.
Neither central atom retains electrons.

check.stem: State the shape and bond angle of BeCl2.
check.modelAnswer: Linear, with a bond angle of 180 degrees.

check.stem: State the shape and bond angle of BCl3.
check.modelAnswer: Trigonal planar, with bond angles of 120 degrees.

check.stem: Explain why electron deficiency in BeCl2 and BCl3 does not distort their shapes.
check.modelAnswer: Shape is set by repulsion among the electron domains present; with no lone pairs competing, the bonding domains alone spread evenly - two to 180, three to 120 - so the missing octet electrons simply never enter the geometry.

check.stem: A student claims BeCl2 should be bent like water because both have two bonds. Assemble the rebuttal.
check.modelAnswer: Water's oxygen carries two lone pairs that squeeze its bonds to 104.5-ish geometry; beryllium in BeCl2 has no lone pairs at all, so its two domains spread to the full 180 degree line.

lessons.title: The tetrahedral family: CH4, NH3, NH4+
lessons.opening: Four electron domains build tetrahedra - and the fourth member of the family shows how lone pairs bend the rules. Methane's four bonds spread to the full 109.5 degrees; ammonia's lone pair squeezes its three bonds down to 107 in a trigonal pyramid; the ammonium ion, its lone pair spent on a dative bond to H+, snaps back to a perfect tetrahedral 109.5.
keyPoints: Methane's carbon has 4 valence electrons, all bonding four hydrogens with no lone pairs.
CH4 is tetrahedral with a bond angle of 109.5 degrees.
Ammonia's nitrogen bonds three hydrogens and keeps one lone pair, giving a trigonal pyramid at 107 degrees.
The lone pair's extra repulsion squeezes NH3's angle below the tetrahedral value.
NH4+ uses its fourth pair in a dative bond, restoring a tetrahedral 109.5 like CH4.

low.restatement: Four bonds sit at 109.5; swap one bond for a lone pair and the angle drops to 107; spend that lone pair on a dative bond and the 109.5 returns.
low.analogy: Four equal sofa cushions spread evenly; replace one with a fatter cushion (lone pair) and the others lean away; swap the fat cushion back and the even spread returns.
low.examPointer: The 107 versus 109.5 contrast is the classic mark: attribute the difference to lone-pair repulsion, not to nitrogen's identity.

medium.restatement: Domain accounting decides the angle: four equal bonding domains give 109.5, but a lone pair's denser cloud presses the remaining bonds together (107 in NH3); donating that pair to a proton converts it into an ordinary bonding domain, and the tetrahedral angle is restored in NH4+.
medium.analogy: A parking bay: four equal cars fit evenly; an oversized van (lone pair) forces neighbours closer; remove the van for a standard car (dative bond) and even spacing returns.
medium.examPointer: For NH4+, say 'dative covalent bond from nitrogen's pair to H+' - the dative language is part of the mark.

check.stem: What is the bond angle in methane?

options.explanation: Four equal bonding domains spread tetrahedrally.
That is ammonia's squeezed angle.
That is the planar value.
That is linear geometry.

check.stem: Why does NH3 show a smaller bond angle than CH4?

options.text: Its lone pair repels more strongly than a bonding pair, squeezing the three bonds to 107
options.explanation: The concentrated lone cloud presses the bonds together.

options.text: Nitrogen has fewer electrons than carbon
options.explanation: Nitrogen has more, and the count is not the mechanism.

options.text: Hydrogen atoms repel each other unusually
options.explanation: The repulsion pattern is normal.
NH3 is a trigonal pyramid in 3D.

check.stem: With three bonds and one lone pair on nitrogen, which shape does NH3 adopt?

options.explanation: Three bonds plus one lone pair on nitrogen.
The domain count is four but one is a lone pair; the molecular shape is pyramidal.
That needs three bonding domains only.
Three bonds cannot be linear.

check.stem: Why is NH4+ tetrahedral with a 109.5 degree angle like CH4?

options.text: Its lone pair became a dative bond, so all four domains are bonding pairs
options.explanation: Four equal domains spread to the tetrahedral angle.

options.text: The positive charge widens the angle
options.explanation: Charge is not the mechanism; domain type is.
The hydrogens are unchanged.

options.text: It lost its lone pair entirely to space
options.explanation: The pair sits in the N-H dative bond.

check.stem: How many of nitrogen's five valence electrons are bonding, and how many lone, in NH3?

options.text: Three bonding, two lone - one lone pair
options.explanation: The 5-valence ledger splits 3+2.
Nitrogen forms exactly three N-H bonds.
Three hydrogens accept three pairs.
Three bonds exist in the molecule.

check.stem: State the bond angle of CH4 and of NH3.
check.modelAnswer: CH4 is 109.5 degrees; NH3 is squeezed to 107 degrees by its lone pair.

check.stem: State the shape of NH4+ and the bond type that completes its fourth domain.
check.modelAnswer: NH4+ is tetrahedral, with nitrogen's pair donated as a dative covalent bond to H+ completing the fourth domain.

check.stem: Explain why spending the lone pair restores the tetrahedral angle in NH4+.
check.modelAnswer: A lone pair's dense cloud repels harder than any bond pair, but once donated it becomes an ordinary N-H bonding domain; four equal bonding domains then spread to the standard 109.5 tetrahedral angle.

check.stem: Trace the angle change from CH4 to NH3 to NH4+ and give the cause at each step.
check.modelAnswer: 109.5 (four equal bonds) falls to 107 when one bond becomes a lone pair whose stronger repulsion squeezes the rest, then returns to 109.5 when that lone pair is donated to H+ as a dative bond, restoring four equal domains.

lessons.title: Bipyramids, planar sheets and electron audits
lessons.opening: Expanded domains and double bonds complete the catalogue. Phosphorus pentachloride spends all five valence electrons on bonds, building a trigonal bipyramid with angles of 120 and 90. Ethene audits to twelve electrons: eight in four C-H bonds, four in the C=C, leaving each carbon three electron-density regions and a trigonal planar shape.
keyPoints: Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons, all bonding chlorine with no lone pairs.
PCl5(g) is trigonal (triangular) bipyramidal with bond angles of 120 and 90 degrees.
Ethene's electrons audit: 12 total, 8 in the four C-H bonds, 4 in the C=C.
Each ethene carbon has three regions of electron density, giving an overall trigonal planar shape.
Electron audits - counting valence electrons into bonds and pairs - are the working method for every shape prediction.

low.restatement: Five bonds fan into a bipyramid (120 between the flat three, 90 to the axial two); ethene's carbon counts three regions per atom and sits flat at 120.
low.analogy: A five-armed starfish spreads two arms upright and three along the seabed; a three-armed one lies perfectly flat.
low.examPointer: PCl5 has TWO angles - quote both 120 and 90; a single-angle answer is half an answer.

medium.restatement: The audit method generalises: total the valence electrons, assign them to bonds and pairs, then read the domain count per central atom - five domains make the bipyramid, three make the planar sheet, and a double bond counts as one region of density.
medium.analogy: A ledger closing: every electron assigned to its account (bond or lone pair), then the account count - not the money - sets the building's floor plan.
medium.examPointer: In ethene, remember the double bond is one region: three regions per carbon, not four.

check.stem: What shape does PCl5(g) adopt?

options.explanation: Five bonding domains with no lone pairs.
That fits four domains, not five.
That fits three domains.
That fits two domains.

check.stem: Which bond angles does PCl5 carry?

options.explanation: Equatorial pairs at 120, axial at 90.
That is the tetrahedral single angle.
Linear is not this molecule.
That is ammonia's squeezed angle.

check.stem: How many electrons does ethene contain in total?

options.text: Twelve - two carbons at 4 each plus four hydrogens at 1 each

options.explanation: That misses four electrons.
That misses two.
That overcounts by two.

check.stem: How are ethene's twelve electrons distributed?

options.text: Eight in the four C-H bonds and four in the C=C double bond
options.explanation: The audit assigns every electron to a bond.

options.text: Six in C-H and six in C=C
options.explanation: Four C-H bonds cannot hold six electrons.
The four C-H bonds hold eight.

options.text: Eight in C-H and two in C=C
options.explanation: The double bond needs four electrons.

check.stem: Why is each carbon in ethene trigonal planar?

options.text: Each carbon has three regions of electron density - two C-H bonds and the C=C as one region
options.explanation: Three domains spread flat at 120.

options.text: Each carbon has four separate regions
options.explanation: The double bond counts as one region.
Domain geometry, not hydrogen size, decides.
Ethene is neutral.

check.stem: State the shape and both bond angles of PCl5(g).
check.modelAnswer: Trigonal (triangular) bipyramidal, with bond angles of 120 and 90 degrees.

check.stem: State the electron audit of ethene.
check.modelAnswer: Twelve electrons in total: eight in the four C-H bonds and four in the C=C double bond.

check.stem: Explain why a double bond counts as one region of electron density when predicting shape.
check.modelAnswer: Shape follows how domains repel around a central atom, and both pairs of a double bond occupy the same region between the same two atoms; the geometry responds to regions, not to individual pairs.

check.stem: Run the full audit for CO2: total valence electrons, bond assignment and final shape.
check.modelAnswer: Carbon brings 4 and each oxygen 6, totalling 16; two C=O double bonds take all sixteen into bonding; carbon then carries two regions of density, so CO2 is linear.

glossary.definition: Describing a central atom accommodating fewer than eight outer-shell electrons, as in BeCl2 and BCl3.
The five-domain shape of PCl5, with 120 and 90 degree bond angles.
Any bonding domain - single, double or lone pair - counted around a central atom when predicting shape.
